intro: The brain and the immune system signal to each other in both directions. This entry reviews what the immune system does, the classic experiments showing that immune responses can be conditioned, and how acute and chronic stress change immunity and produce cytokine-driven sickness behavior (Figure 33-28). It then surveys immune findings in major depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism, and in Alzheimer disease, HIV infection, multiple sclerosis, chronic fatigue syndrome, Lyme disease and Gulf War syndrome, and closes with the effects of antidepressants and psychosocial interventions on immunity. Update boxes add the infliximab trial in depression, complement C4 and the minocycline trial in schizophrenia, later evidence and agency statements on vaccines and autism, NSAID prevention trials in Alzheimer disease and the current definition of ME/CFS.
objectives: Describe the main functions of the immune system and the role of cytokines as messengers between immunity and the brain.
Explain conditioned immunosuppression and the experiment that demonstrated it.
Explain how the timing, type and duration of stress shape immune effects, and list the features of sickness behavior.
Summarize the immune findings reported in depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism, and their level of certainty.
Describe immune involvement in Alzheimer disease, HIV infection, multiple sclerosis and related disorders.
Explain how antidepressants and psychosocial interventions may alter immune function, and what later anti-inflammatory trials showed.
